2. My camera trap spacing is very small, on average they are 1500 m apart. The MCP of camera array is almost 40 km2, and we counted 10 adult leopards.
When I ask the secr to give me a sigma, it is almost 1400 m and the density would be 7 ind/100 km2.
But I have GPS collar data for a few leopards in my area and the mean diameter of home ranges are almost 15 km (excluding dispersing collared individuals which roamed massive areas and I excluded it from my mean diameter calculations). So, I fixed the sigma when I fit models to 10000 m, the density crashed to 0.7 ind/100 km2.
My main concern is I am confused which one is correct. 7 ind/100 km2 density is reasonable for me, but I think it is underestimating the sigma, probably due to short distance between camera traps. But I do not know how to make best of my GPS collar data here.
Also, I have seen different justifiction to calculate buffer based on sigma (2/3/4* sigma) which is also another source of confusion.
Any thought is highly appreciated.
Mohammad

messages.subject: Re: Multi-session model
messages.body_plain:
It's up to you whether you fit a model with constant density (the default D tilde 1) or session-specific density (D tilde session). Why should a small mammal not have density 7/ha?
Murray

messages.subject: Re: GPS data and sigma/buffer
messages.body_plain:
Please read the documentation. I think you have the usage codes in the wrong place - they precede covariates. Sigma 1400 m is compatible with range diam 15 km (factor is about 5).
Murray

Sent from my Samsung Galaxy smartphone.

I have data from series of camera traps across a sampling region.
I suspect my target species to have home ranges in that dont overlap, and I have an approximation of where these home ranges are but I am not 100% sure.
I want to fit several SECR models, is it possible to create one SECR model that treats the data so that there are no territories and then another SECR model that includes a covariate for camera if they fall within one of th territories that I suspect.  So if for example I suspect there are 3 territories, for each camera, I could add a covariate value of 1 - 3 if the camera was placed in one of the three territories.  Or 4 if it is none and then compare the models using AIC?
Is this possible
Many Thanks

messages.subject: Effect of Occasion Length on Estimated Denstiy
messages.subject_clean: Effect of Occasion Length on Estimated Denstiy
messages.body_plain:
Hi Everyone,

I'm working with some camera trap data for mountain lions, and I was curious about how estimated density may be affected by sampling occasion length? For all passive detectors, we are continuously sampling a population and during analysis, we break this sampling into discrete time periods. Usually, we want to bin time into the shortest possible interval while maintaining independence between occasions. Yet, creating longer occasions may be necessary with sparse data to ensure capture probabilities aren't so low that parameter estimation becomes an issue.

Given that, I was curious how 10 19-day occasions might affect an estimate compared to 14 14-day or 26 7-day occasions? Since camera traps collect count information, I was thinking there wouldn't be too much of an effect given you don't lose any capture information. Instead, the biggest concern would be if detection probability fluctuated quite frequently and a shorter occasion length would allow you to more accurately represent that variation.
I've read Borchers et al.'s (2014) paper on continuous-time models, and their findings seem to suggest shorter occasions would be better in order to approximate continuous time. Yet, they also compared their CT model to binary data, which would contain less capture information than count data.

Is my reasoning flawed? Any thoughts or suggestions on the matter would be greatly appreciated. Thanks for your time and take care.

Best,

Matt

messages.subject_clean: Effect of Occasion Length on Estimated Denstiy
messages.body_plain:
Hi Matt

If you are fitting a Poisson count model then lumping of occasions is safe, as you suggest. One could check this by looking at the likelihood, but there's an example below with a simulated dataset that is fairly convincing. Count data clearly contain more information than the same data reduced to binary - a point made also for binomial counts in App A of our 2009 'pattern' paper.

I'm not aware of evidence that sparseness (number of detections per occasion) is a problem in itself (what matters is the total number of individuals and redetections).

Notice that I used detectfn = 'HHN' (halfnormal on the hazard scale). I haven't recently tested 'HN' etc.

Collapsing occasions of course limits your ability to model temporal change in lambda0 etc., but in my experience that is seldom a problem.

Murray

library(secr)
grid <- make.grid(nx = 8, ny = 8, detector = "count")
CH1 <- sim.capthist(grid, popn = list(D = 10, buffer = 100, Ndist = "fixed"),
                   detectfn = 'HHN', noccasions = 26 * 7, seed = 12349,
                   detectpar = list(lambda0 = 0.002, sigma = 20))

## The raw data are very sparse at the level of daily 'occasions', even when we sum
## across detectors:
table(apply(CH1,1:2,sum))
#
# 0    1
# 5929   77

## now collapse by week, by fortnight, or entire survey:
CH7 <- reduce(CH1, by = 7)
CH14 <- reduce(CH1, by = 14)
CHall <- reduce(CH1, by = "all")

## the numbers of detections and individuals are unaffected:
summary(CH1)
summary(CHall)

fit1 <- secr.fit(CH1, detectfn = 'HHN', biasLimit = NA, trace = FALSE)
fit7 <- secr.fit(CH7, detectfn = 'HHN', biasLimit = NA, trace = FALSE)
fit14 <- secr.fit(CH14, detectfn = 'HHN', biasLimit = NA, trace = FALSE)
fitall <- secr.fit(CHall, detectfn = 'HHN', biasLimit = NA, trace = FALSE)
fits <- secrlist(fit1 = fit1, fit7 = fit7, fit14 = fit14, fitall = fitall)

## estimates of density are the same except for slight numerical effects
predict(fits)
# $fit1
# link estimate SE.estimate      lcl     ucl
# D        log  9.90150    1.888975  6.83535 14.3430
# lambda0  log  0.00241    0.000498  0.00161  0.0036
# sigma    log 20.87248    1.913921 17.44559 24.9725
#
# $fit7
# link estimate SE.estimate     lcl     ucl
# D        log   9.9015     1.88897  6.8353 14.3430
# lambda0  log   0.0175     0.00362  0.0117  0.0262
# sigma    log  20.8725     1.91392 17.4456 24.9725
#
# $fit14
# link estimate SE.estimate     lcl     ucl
# D        log   9.9015     1.88898  6.8354 14.3431
# lambda0  log   0.0337     0.00697  0.0226  0.0503
# sigma    log  20.8725     1.91392 17.4456 24.9725
#
# $fitall
# link estimate SE.estimate      lcl     ucl
# D        log  9.90146    1.888970  6.83532 14.3430
# lambda0  log  0.00241    0.000498  0.00161  0.0036
# sigma    log 20.87249    1.913924 17.44560 24.9725

## However, the estimate of lambda0 varies for weekly and fortnightly intervals.
## The agreement between the daily and all-occasion lambda0-hat is due to a quirk of
## reduce.capthist: a usage attribute is constructed when by = "all"; the usage matrix
## has effort 26 x 7 = 182 at each detector and the fitted lambda0-hat is scaled to a
## daily value (unless you set ignoreusage).

## Collapsing the data to a single occasion is much faster (using secr 3.0.3 on a slowish laptop)
sapply(fits, '[[', 'proctime')
# fit1.elapsed   fit7.elapsed  fit14.elapsed fitall.elapsed
# 1208.42         151.25          58.97          20.49

Since camera traps collect count information, I was thinking there wouldn't be too much of an effect given you don't lose any capture information. Instead, the biggest concern would be if detection probability fluctuated quite frequently and a shorter occasion length would allow you to more accurately represent that variation.
> I've read Borchers et al.'s (2014) paper on continuous-time models, and their findings seem to suggest shorter occasions would be better in order to approximate continuous time. Yet, they also compared their CT model to binary data, which would contain less capture information than count data.
>
> Is my reasoning flawed? Any thoughts or suggestions on the matter would be greatly appreciated. Thanks for your time and take care.
>
> Best,
>
> Matt

messages.body_plain:
Hello everyone,

This is my first time posting to this forum and I'm excited to hear more about your experiences using SECR.

I'm currently a grad student in wildlife biology collecting fecal samples left behind by elk harems to estimate abundance in distinct regions throughout my study area. I haven't used SECR modeling yet however I was wondering if it can help answer a research question I have with my data. From what I've gathered, SECR is typically used to estimate density using a capture history within a home range. Has it ever been used to inform sampling protocols to anyone's knowledge?

Here's where I'm coming from: I'm using GPS data from collared elk to locate where a harem has been and where to find scat from the group (judgement sampling). These locations are based on where the elk have recently been (<week for genetic amplification reasons). I was wondering if the data I collect at these sites (# of elk identified, detecting scat, etc.) can be used to model locations or probability of detection of scat across their home range and thus inform sampling in the absence of collar data.

I appreciate any feedback you may have to this question.

Thanks.
